extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecution practitioners as reference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and supporting patent eligibility (35 U.S.C. 101) rejections, including how to identify judicial exceptions in claims, evaluate additional claim elements under Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B, and meet evidentiary requirements. Applies to examiners composing first actions and final rejections and using prescribed form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception. The rejection must explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information about Step 2A of the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must identify the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the exception and provide a reasoned rationale explaining why those limitations are a judicial exception. If the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. Include sample explanation language where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify abstract idea as recited and justify grouping (abstract idea specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation does not fall within those groupings, use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (MPEP § 2106.04 IV) and provide justification. Optionally cite appropriate court decisions that support the identification of the abstract idea, but examiners should be familiar with cited decisions and ensure the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts. Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless the facts match uniquely. A sample explanation is provided (e.g., comparing collected information to a threshold is a 'mental process').

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify law of nature or natural phenomenon as recited and provide reasoned rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify it as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a factual explanation tying the claim language to natural consequences or occurrences (examples: a correlation X that describes a consequence of natural processes; something that occurs in nature and exists apart from human action). See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for more information and sample explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify product of nature exceptions and analyze markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain lack of marked differences in structure, function, or properties. Provide examples (e.g., isolated DNA segment conveying same genetic information). See MPEP § 2106.04(b)-(c) for guidance on the markedly different characteristics analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do or do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation should address the additional elements both individually and in combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they are well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr), so address combination-level effects carefully. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concluding particular limitations are well understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the specified evidentiary options (A–D). Provide reasoned analysis for why the additional elements do not add a meaningful limitation, and explain both individual limitations and their combination. See MPEP § 2106.05 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection only when conclusion is readily apparent; explain rationale for applicant response
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why the additional elements do integrate an exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. It is a best practice to consult the specification to identify elements that could be added to make the claim eligible and suggest them in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components and generic computing functions guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind courts have held that combinations of generic computer components can sometimes be 'significantly more' (e.g., DDR Holdings). Refer to MPEP § 2106.05(f) for examples of generic computing functions that courts have found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer and to MPEP § 2106.05(d) for well-understood/conventional activities considerations. Explain why the recited computer elements are merely generic implementation if so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and mere field-of-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples and reasons (e.g., storing data to a process of computing area does not add meaningful limitation; placing a product of nature in a test tube is nominal token activity). Cite relevant precedent (Parker v. Flook) and MPEP subsections 2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h). Explain that merely employing well-known computer functions or limiting use to one environment typically is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: no evidence required for Step 2A Prong One
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions have identified abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Thus for Step 2A Prong One, examiner need not cite publications, affidavits, or declarations to find that a claim recites a judicial exception. Cite supporting case law listed in the guidance if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary threshold for Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B when asserting well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support findings that an exception is not integrated or that additional elements do not amount to significantly more—unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the listed options (A–D). See case law (e.g., Berkheimer) recognizing underlying factual issues may exist for such determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support Option A: specification or applicant statement showing well-understood, routine, conventional nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may support a finding that additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional by citing an express statement in the specification or a statement made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification demonstrates the nature when it describes the element as well-understood, routine or conventional (or equivalent), as a commercially available product, or in a manner indicating such elements are sufficiently well-known that particulars need not be described to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A finding cannot be based solely on specification silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support Option B: citation to court decisions showing conventional nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may cite one or more court decisions that note the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s) to support the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality. It is not sufficient that elements are merely similar. Court decisions cited do not imply all computer functions are conventional; courts have sometimes found generic computer combinations to be significantly more (DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support Option C: citation to a publication demonstrating wide prevalence/common use
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may cite an appropriate publication (book, manual, review article, or other source describing the state of the art) that demonstrates the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document being a 'printed publication' under 35 U.S.C. 102 is a distinct inquiry from demonstrating 'well-understood, routine, conventional' activity. A single patent or published application is generally insufficient unless it demonstrates wide prevalence; the publication must show the elements are so well-known that they need not be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Examples and cautions provided (e.g., Exergen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support Option D: examiner taking official notice of conventional nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take official notice of the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of additional elements when certain based on the examiner's personal knowledge that the elements represent widely prevalent or common activity in the relevant art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official notice only when the examiner is certain, and follow procedures for taking official notice and addressing applicant challenges per MPEP § 2144.03. Example: taking official notice that a generic computer component using the Internet to gather data is well-understood, routine, conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections and required structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and 7.05.017) for rejections based on failure to claim statutory categories or directed to a judicial exception without an inventive concept/significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections. 7.05 is a heading-only paragraph that must be preceded/followed by specific content. 7.05.016 must identify the type of exception, how it is recited, why it is not integrated into a practical application, and why additional elements do not add significantly more. If the exception is a 'tentative abstract idea' use 7.05.017 in addition and include TC Director signature. Follow the Examiner Notes for bracketed content and sequencing (see page text for bracket instructions and examples).
